topic: The Magic of Fair Sharing: From Earth's Temperature to the Stolen Necklace Problem
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in mathematics and topology

outline.topic: The Magic of Fair Sharing: From Earth's Temperature to the Stolen Necklace Problem
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in mathematics and topology

sections.title: The Thief's Dilemma: The Stolen Necklace Problem
sections.content: Introduce a discrete combinatorial problem: Two thieves steal a necklace made of different types of precious beads (e.g., rubies and emeralds). They want to split the necklace so that each gets exactly half of each type of bead. What is the minimum number of cuts required?
sections.example: Visualize a string of 10 red beads and 8 green beads. Instead of cutting every single bead, can we find a way to make just 2 cuts to satisfy both thieves?

sections.title: Prerequisite: Antipodal Points and Continuous Mapping
sections.content: Define 'antipodal points' as points directly opposite each other on a circle or sphere. Introduce the concept of a continuous function mapping a higher-dimensional shape to a lower-dimensional value (like mapping a point on Earth to its temperature).
sections.example: Imagine a thermometer moving around a circular wire. As it moves, the temperature changes smoothly without any sudden jumps.

sections.title: The 1D Borsuk-Ulam: The Equator Example
sections.content: Explain the simplest form of the theorem: On any circle (the equator), there must exist at least one pair of opposite points with the exact same temperature. Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that the difference function f(x) - f(-x) must cross zero.
sections.example: An animated Earth rotates. We highlight two opposite points on the equator. As they spin, their temperatures eventually match perfectly at at least two spots.

sections.title: The Formal Theorem: Scaling Up Dimensions
sections.content: State the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem: For any continuous function mapping an n-sphere to n-dimensional Euclidean space, there exists a pair of antipodal points that map to the same value. Explain that for a 2D sphere (Earth), there are two opposite spots with the same temperature AND the same atmospheric pressure.
sections.example: A 3D globe is flattened into a 2D weather map. We use a crosshair to find the 'magic' antipodal points where (Temp, Pressure) = (Temp, Pressure).

sections.title: The Solution: Connecting Topology to Beads
sections.content: Connect the theorem back to the necklace. We represent the 'cuts' as positions on a sphere. By defining a function that measures how much of each bead type Thief A gets, we can prove that there is a configuration where the difference between Thief A and Thief B's loot is zero for all bead types.
sections.example: An animation converts the necklace into a mathematical space. For 'k' types of beads, the theorem proves we only need 'k' cuts to make a perfect split. If there are 2 types of beads, 2 cuts always suffice.

sections.title: Summary and Real-world Intuition
sections.content: Wrap up by highlighting how abstract topology (the study of shapes) provides elegant solutions to discrete problems (counting beads). Emphasize that continuity is the key that unlocks fairness.
sections.example: A final graphic shows the two thieves happily walking away with their perfectly equal shares of rubies and emeralds, thanks to the Borsuk-Ulam theorem.

storyboard.title: The Thief's Dilemma: The Stolen Necklace Problem
lecture_lines: Two thieves steal a necklace with different beads.
They want to split each bead type equally.
How many cuts are needed for a fair share?
Imagine ten red and eight green beads.
Can we solve this with just two cuts?
animations: Show a linear sequence of 18 beads: 10 red (#FF0000) and 8 green (#00FF00) in a random order.
Highlight two figures labeled Thief A (#FFD700) and Thief B (#ADFF2F) with 50/50 targets.
Show many vertical lines cutting every single bead, showing a tedious but fair split.
Remove many lines and place exactly two orange (#FFA500) cutting markers on the necklace.
Necklace segments move to thieves, each receiving 5 red and 4 green beads.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Antipodal Points and Continuous Mapping
lecture_lines: Antipodal points are directly opposite on a circle.
Continuous functions map points to values like temperature.
Temperature changes smoothly along the circular wire.
animations: A circle appears with two diametrically opposite points highlighted in blue (#00BFFF) and labeled 'Antipodal'.
A temperature scale appears; as one point moves around the circle, its temperature value fluctuates smoothly.
A mapping arrow from the circle to a 1D line is shown, labeled 'Continuous Function' (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The 1D Borsuk-Ulam: The Equator Example
lecture_lines: On the equator, two opposite points share a temperature.
Define a function for the temperature difference at opposites.
If the difference flips sign, it must hit zero.
This zero point means temperatures are exactly equal.
This is the Intermediate Value Theorem in action.
animations: A spinning Earth globe is shown with the Equator line highlighted in gold (#FFD700).
Two antipodal points on the equator show dynamic temperature values T and T'.
A graph of g(x) = T(x) - T(-x) appears below the globe, showing a continuous curve.
As the points rotate, the graph is shown crossing the zero line (#FFFFFF).
Two specific antipodal points are highlighted where T = T', marked with stars (#FFFF00).

storyboard.title: The Formal Theorem: Scaling Up Dimensions
lecture_lines: Borsuk-Ulam maps an n-sphere to n-dimensional space.
On Earth, two opposites share temperature and pressure.
Every continuous mapping has a matching antipodal pair.
animations: Text: 'For f: S^n -> R^n, exists x s.t. f(x) = f(-x)' appears in white (#FFFFFF).
A 2D sphere (Earth) shows two values at each point: Temperature (#FF4500) and Pressure (#1E90FF).
A scanning crosshair finds a pair of antipodal points where both values match perfectly.

storyboard.title: The Solution: Connecting Topology to Beads
lecture_lines: We map necklace cuts to points on a sphere.
A function measures the bead difference for one thief.
For k bead types, k cuts ensure a perfect split.
Two cuts always divide two bead types fairly.
Topology guarantees a solution for any number of types.
animations: Represent the necklace as a unit interval [0, 1] with bead densities.
Show a transformation of the interval into a 2D sphere representation for 'cuts'.
Define a mapping where the output is the 'surplus' of each bead type for Thief A.
Apply the theorem: a zero-crossing exists for both bead types simultaneously.
Display the necklace being cut at those two specific spots, resulting in perfect equity.

storyboard.title: Summary and Real-world Intuition
lecture_lines: Topology provides elegant solutions to discrete problems.
Continuity ensures fairness in complex sharing scenarios.
Mathematical beauty solves the thieves' difficult dilemma.
animations: Icons of a necklace and a sphere are linked with a 'Topology' bridge (#DA70D6).
Text 'Continuity is the Key' flashes in bright cyan (#00FFFF).
The two thieves from Section 1 shake hands over their equal bead piles.
